fields.sample_size: 153 localities of the municipality (76 urban and 77 rural by 2,500-inhabitant rule; 63 urban, 44 rural and 46 peripheral in the authors' three-way typology); 153 key-informant surveys (one per locality: neighbourhood presidents, municipal agents, police agents) and 68 semi-structured interviews with SAPAHUA and municipal staff and presidents of independent water systems; population 78,313 (56,163 urban, 22,150 rural)
fields.effect_measure: descriptive counts and percentages of localities and population by water-supply type, with mean monthly cost by type (Table 2); mixed-methods triangulation; no inferential statistics
fields.effect_estimate: Of 153 localities, 88 are supplied by the municipal operator SAPAHUA (70.6% of the population, 55,339 inhabitants; 86 of the 88 have sewers), 38 by community-run Independent Water Systems (SIA; 15 have sewers, 23 do not), 17 by water trucks (11.6% of the population, 9,078 inhabitants; 14 of 17 outside the sewer network) and 10 by private wells (1,637 inhabitants). SIA users report the lowest mean monthly cost (91 pesos) against 126 pesos for SAPAHUA users; households that self-supply by trucks or wells report higher spending. Where the municipality does not serve, residents organise their own systems, but the capacity to do so is limited by locality size and distance from the urban area. The authors conclude that official data ignore discontinuity of access and call for recognising SIAs and self-supply in municipal and higher-level policy.

fields.exact_location: Table 1 (methods); Results text on the four management types and Table 2 (monthly cost); Conclusions; Investigaciones Geográficas 108:e60529

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a mixed-methods geodemographic case study of domestic water supply in one Mexican municipality (153 localities, 153 key-informant surveys and 68 interviews); read in full text 2026-10-04. Descriptive counts and percentages by supply type; no inferential statistics.
